structured_extraction.program_description: A program that allows businesses to quickly access their facilities after a major emergency or disaster. Employees receive secure identification cards that are recognized by the Baltimore Police Department, allowing them to enter restricted areas during emergencies to assess damage, maintain critical systems, meet legal obligations, and secure important records and data.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Pre-event credentialing program that issues secure identification cards to critical business employees. Cards are recognized by the Baltimore Police Department and permit cardholders to access restricted areas following a declared emergency or disaster.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore-based businesses of all types and sizes that want to ensure their critical employees can rapidly access facilities following a major emergency or catastrophic event.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Access to business facilities following emergencies to assess damage, maintain core IT systems, meet regulatory obligations, and secure or remove vital records and data.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City
requirements_list: Must be a Baltimore-based business
Must identify critical business employees for credentialing
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Visit www.ceas.com to learn more and enroll in the pre-event credentialing program.

structured_extraction.program_description: The City provides capital support to cultural organizations that promote arts and culture in Baltimore City. Organizations can apply every two years for General Obligation bonds to fund eligible capital improvements to their facilities.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: General Obligation bonds for capital improvements distributed on a reimbursement basis. Total of $1 million per year is available for FY2026 and FY2027. Individual awards will not exceed $200,000 over two years. Typical awards range between $50,000 to $100,000 over a two-year period. FY26 funds become available July 1, 2025 and FY27 funds become available July 1, 2026. Funds are provided on a reimbursement basis; applicants submit invoices to the Department of Planning which are processed by the Department of Finance - Bureau of Accounting and Payroll Services.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Registered non-profit museums, galleries, theaters, and other arts or cultural venues within designated arts and entertainment districts throughout Baltimore City that are open to the general public.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Capital improvements to cultural facilities including building systems (roof, HVAC, windows, elevators), interior and exterior renovations, fire protection systems, ADA accessibility improvements, upgrades to plazas or entrances, museum or exhibit expansions, and related preliminary studies and surveys. Projects must have a minimum 15-year service life and cost at least $50,000.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Open to organizations with physical locations in Baltimore City. Organizations must be located within designated arts and entertainment districts or be museums, galleries, theaters, or other arts or cultural venues.
requirements_list: Must be a registered non-profit in good standing with the State Department of Assessment and Taxation
Must have a physical location in Baltimore City
Must own the facility or have a minimum 15-year lease with primary responsibility for capital improvements
Facility must be open to the general public
Projects must cost at least $50,000
Projects must have a minimum 15-year service life
Projects cannot be repairs or maintenance items costing less than $100,000 or of an emergency nature
Projects cannot include vehicular equipment or salaries except those properly capitalized as project costs
Projects cannot support specific religious or other affiliations, political actions, causes, advocacy, or parties
Expenses cannot be incurred until after final approval of the budget by City Council
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Applications open February 18, 2025. Information sessions held March 6, 2025 at 10:00 am and March 18, 2025 at 2:00 pm via WebEx. Full applications due April 30, 2025, submitted in Microsoft Word format to Shakia Word at shakia.word@baltimorecity.gov. Applications include sections on contact information, project information, project schedule, cost estimates, funding sources, facility information, organization financials, and population served. Inter-agency review panel reviews applications in May 2025. Organizations are notified of awards on June 23, 2025. Award amounts are determined by the Director of Planning and must be approved in the capital budget. Grant agreements must be signed by grantee, Department of Planning, and Law Department and approved by the Board of Estimates before funds are available.

structured_extraction.program_description: A business-driven training strategy that assists employers with meeting the cost of training new employees in hard-to-fill positions. Employers or groups of employers can provide occupational skills tailored to their specific needs, resulting in a more productive and efficient workforce.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: MOED will reimburse businesses up to 50 percent of the training costs, which may include wages, tools, uniforms, and training courses. Training can be provided by the employer or by a WIOA Eligible Training Provider. MOED also provides marketing, recruitment, and pre-screening of applicants through its career center services.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Employers seeking to train new hires in hard-to-fill positions across all industries.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Training costs including wages, tools, uniforms, and training courses for new employees in hard-to-fill positions.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City
requirements_list: Training positions must be full-time permanent positions
Wages must be $10 per hour or higher
Businesses must commit to hiring trainees who successfully complete the training program
Training can be provided by the employer or a WIOA Eligible Training Provider
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Get started by completing the Customized Training/OJT Business Application through the MOED website.

structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free or low-cost food scrap drop-off service for residents participating in the pilot program.

structured_extraction.program_name: Department of Housing and Community Development Weatherization Assistance Program
structured_extraction.program_description: This program helps low-income households in Baltimore City reduce energy expenses by installing energy conservation materials and products such as weatherstripping, insulation, and efficient heating systems to lower utility bills. It offers weatherization and energy efficiency improvements to homes, helping low-income residents improve home heating and reduce energy costs. The program is administered through the DHCD Division of Homeownership and Housing Preservation.
list_of_relevant_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Provides free or subsidized installation of energy conservation materials and products such as weatherstripping, insulation, efficient heating systems, and other measures to reduce utility costs. Weatherization or energy efficiency programs are available for low-income homeowners to improve home heating and reduce energy costs. Some programs provide assistance as a grant, while others offer forgivable or deferred loans. Forgivable loans are forgiven after five years if the applicant lives in their home as their primary residence during that time. Deferred loans are due back to the City when the home is sold and are paid from the profit of the sale.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Low-income homeowners and renters in Baltimore City with household incomes at or below 200% of the Federal Poverty Level seeking to reduce energy expenses and utility bills.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Energy conservation materials, weatherization work, heating system improvements, insulation, weatherstripping, and other energy efficiency measures to reduce utility costs.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available to residents of Baltimore City only. For homeowners, the deed must be in the applicant's name. For renters, landlord consent may be required.

Household income at or below 200% of Federal Poverty Level
For homeowners: deed must be in applicant's name
For homeowners: must be current on mortgage payments (if applicable)
For homeowners: must be current on property taxes
For homeowners: must be current on ground rent payments (if applicable)
For homeowners: must have homeowner's insurance
For homeowners: no outstanding judgments against household members
For homeowners: no bankruptcy declared in the last seven years
For homeowners: no active foreclosure efforts on property
For renters: landlord/apartment complex contact information required
Pre-application submission required to determine program eligibility
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Submit a pre-application form online at https://portal.neighborlysoftware.com/BALTIMOREMD/participant or contact the LIGHT Intake & Assessment Unit. The LIGHT Intake & Assessment Unit is located at 417 East Fayette Street, Suite 1125, Baltimore, MD 21202. LIGHT Coordinators will review the pre-application to determine which home repair programs the applicant may be eligible for. If eligible, applicants will be requested to submit a full application with supporting documents. Once submitted, the program will review the full application and determine final eligibility. Some programs have waiting lists. Contact (410) 396-3023 or call 311 for assistance. In-person assistance is available at various city offices and community organizations.

structured_extraction.program_description: A federally funded congregate nutrition program that provides nutritious meals in a social dining setting for seniors. The program promotes health, reduces isolation, and offers educational events, activities, and social opportunities.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program provides free nutritious meals (lunch or dinner) at congregate dining sites throughout Baltimore City. Participants can make optional confidential donations (suggested at $1.25 for regular meals and $2.00 for kosher meals). There are more than 50 sites offering the program, including options for kosher and Korean meals.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Seniors 60 years of age or older and their spouses regardless of age. Disabled persons younger than 60 may participate if they reside in a residential building where an Eating Together meal program is in operation.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Nutritious meals (lunch or dinner) at congregate dining sites.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City only. More than 50 Eating Together sites are located throughout Baltimore City.

Disabled persons younger than 60 may participate if they reside in a residential building where the program operates
Must complete a registration form to participate
Must swipe membership card to attend meals
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Complete a registration form to join the program. Upon registration, participants receive a membership card to swipe each time they attend a meal. Menus are posted monthly to allow participants to reserve meals on desired dates.

structured_extraction.program_description: A competitive grant program administered by the Mayor's Office of Homeless Services to fund the operation of emergency homeless shelter sites that provide dignified residential settings and services to help people experiencing homelessness transition to housing stability within Baltimore City's Continuum of Care.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Competitive grant funding for operating emergency homeless shelter sites serving persons experiencing homelessness in Baltimore City. Three shelter projects available: (1) Single Men/Single Women at 620 Fallsway with 175 male beds, 75 female beds, plus 15 overflow beds each; (2) Single Women/Families at 1200 N. Fremont Avenue with 70 female beds, 8 family beds, plus overflow capacity (60 female, 50 male, 40 family); (3) Families at privately-owned site TBD with 150 family beds. Performance period: July 1, 2020 through June 30, 2021. Applicants may apply to one, a combination, or all three projects. Funding derives from federal (HUD Emergency Solutions Grant), state (Maryland Homelessness Solutions Program, DSS Shelter Program), and local (City General Fund) sources. Providers must submit monthly expenditure reports and are reimbursed monthly for expenses. Minimum 10% match requirement (cash, in-kind services, or donated materials). Services include shelter operations (maintenance, food service, janitorial, monitoring), case management, complaint response, data collection, linkage to community support, and supportive services aligned with Baltimore Continuum of Care Action Plan.
structured_extraction.contact_name: Wade Carver; Angela D. McCauley; Jay Wilson
structured_extraction.program_audience: Registered non-profit 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organizations and Baltimore City agencies seeking to operate emergency homeless shelter services. Organizations must be registered with the State of Maryland and the U.S. Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and in good standing with the State of Maryland.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Funds support the operation of emergency homeless shelter sites providing dignified residential settings and supportive services to assist people experiencing homelessness in transitioning to housing stability. Services include management of day-to-day shelter operations (basic maintenance, certified food services, janitorial services, shelter monitoring), case management, complaint response/monitoring, data collection and entry, linkage and connection to other community support, and supportive services. All services must align with the Baltimore Continuum of Care Action Plan and follow Housing First principles.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City only. Three specific shelter locations: (1) 620 Fallsway, Baltimore, MD 21202 for Single Men/Single Women shelter; (2) 1200 N. Fremont Avenue, Baltimore, MD 21217 for Single Women/Families shelter; (3) One privately-owned site location to be determined for Families shelter. Providers must maintain an office within Baltimore City of sufficient size to support management of homeless services network and provide space for staff trainings, meetings, and files.

structured_extraction.program_description: The program assists Baltimore City residents whose homes are facing foreclosure or eviction due to economic hardship. Assistance is provided as a direct grant to pay past due mortgage charges, overdue rent, homeowner's insurance, property taxes, and water bills. Payments can be applied toward arrearages for the most recent three-month period. The City has designated $2,000,000 for EMHAP, estimated to support between 100 to 300 households, and funds are distributed on a first-come, first-served basis until all funds are committed.
list_of_relevant_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The City has designated $2,000,000 for EMHAP in the form of direct grant payments to cover past due mortgage payments, rent, homeowner's insurance, property taxes, and water bills. Income limits are based on 80% Area Median Income (AMI) and vary by household size: 1 person $93,800, 2 people $137,550, 3 people $129,250, 4 people $120,900, 5 people $72,950, 6 people $104,200, 7 people $112,550, 8 people $83,400. Funds are estimated to support between 100 to 300 households. Payments apply toward arrearages for the most recent three-month period. The program operates on a first-come, first-served basis until all funds are committed.

structured_extraction.program_description: Federal emergency funding from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development to prevent, prepare for, and respond to the COVID-19 pandemic among individuals and families experiencing homelessness or receiving homeless assistance in Baltimore City. The program strengthens Baltimore City's response to homelessness during COVID-19 by supporting rapid rehousing, homelessness prevention, emergency shelter operations, street outreach, homeless management information systems (HMIS), data management, and program administration activities to mitigate the impacts of COVID-19.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program distributes $15.7 million in total funding across two rounds of ESG-CV awards under the CARES Act (Public Law 116-136). More than $10.7 million (approximately two-thirds) is allocated to rapid rehousing and homelessness prevention. The remainder supports emergency shelter operations, street outreach services, data management systems, and program administration and oversight. In an initial allocation, the City of Baltimore received $6,571,738.00, of which $657,173.80 (10%) was allocated to administration activities including general management, oversight, coordination, and reporting, with remaining funds distributed to Continuum of Care providers for emergency shelter, homelessness prevention, rapid re-housing, and HMIS activities. Funding supports project expansion, emergency supplies (personal protective equipment and cleaning supplies), medical-related expenses, and increased food costs. An additional amendment re-allocated $382,767.00 in ESG Program funds from the Mayor's Office of Homeless Services Prevention Project to Emergency Shelter Operations to increase funding for existing emergency shelter activities.

structured_extraction.program_name: Expedited Reimbursement Program for Sewage Backups
structured_extraction.program_description: A program administered by Baltimore City that reimburses residential customers (homeowners and tenants) for reasonable, documented clean-up, disinfection, and disposal services costs incurred from sewage backups caused by capacity-related wet weather events in the sanitary sewer collection system. Eligible events are those in which at least 1/4 inch of precipitation within 24 hours causes sewer lines to surcharge or overflow. The program is part of Baltimore City's Sanitary Sewer Consent Decree Program and provides up to $5,000 per dwelling unit per event. Applications must be filed within 90 days of the incident, and final determinations are issued within 60 days of receiving all necessary documentation.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program offers up to $5,000 per dwelling unit, per event for reasonable, documented clean-up, disinfection, and disposal services costs, including any insurance deductible paid if demonstrably linked to cleanup and disinfection. Reimbursement is provided as a check after a signed Release is received. If the property is insured against sewage backups, the applicant must first obtain a final written determination from their insurance company before the application is processed. Final determinations are issued within 60 days of receiving all necessary information and documentation. This reimbursement program is authorized under Baltimore City's Modified Consent Decree (which supersedes the 2002 Consent Decree) and is part of the city's efforts to comply with the Clean Water Act and address sewage overflow issues in the Collection System.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Applications must be received within 90 days after the backup; insurance documentation may be provided up to 30 days after receipt from insurer.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore City residential customers, including homeowners and tenants, who have experienced sewage backups or equivalent events caused by capacity-related wet weather events and incurred cleanup, disinfection, and disposal costs.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Documented clean-up, disinfection, and disposal services costs related to sewage backups caused by wet weather events, including any insurance deductible paid if demonstrably linked to cleanup and disinfection. Eligible events are those where at least 1/4 inch of precipitation falls within 24 hours, causing sewer lines to surcharge or overflow.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City residential properties only. Sewage backup events prior to April 6, 2018 are not eligible. The program applies to Building Backups, which are defined as wastewater or sewage releases or backups into a building caused by blockages, flow conditions, or other malfunctions in Baltimore City's Collection System (not caused by blockages or malfunctions in private laterals or private piping systems not owned or operationally controlled by Baltimore, and not resulting from overland surface flooding not emanating from the Collection System).
requirements_list: Must be a City residential customer (homeowner or tenant)
Sewage backup must be caused by a capacity-related wet weather event (at least 1/4 inch of precipitation within 24 hours causing sewer lines to surcharge or overflow)
Sewage backup events prior to April 6, 2018 are not eligible
Application must be filed within 90 days after the incident

If property is insured against backups, must receive a final written determination from insurance company before application is processed; insurance documentation may be provided up to 30 days after receipt from insurer
All documentation provided to and received from insurance company must be included with the application, including proof of any deductible paid
Deductibles are eligible for reimbursement only if costs are demonstrably linked to cleanup and disinfection
Costs must be appropriately documented
If tenant, must provide signed lease copy
If filing on behalf of owner or tenant, must include written proof of power of attorney
Maximum reimbursement is $5,000 per dwelling unit per occurrence
Backup must be a Building Backup (wastewater or sewage backup into the building caused by Collection System malfunction, not from private laterals or overland surface flooding)
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Apply online or submit a completed application by email, certified mail, or commercial delivery to the Baltimore City Department of Public Works, Bureau of Water and Wastewater. Include documentation of all cleanup, disinfection, and disposal expenses, and insurance documentation if applicable. If insured, obtain a final written determination from your insurance company and include all related documentation with your application (insurance documentation may be submitted up to 30 days after receipt from insurer). Applications are processed within 60 days after all necessary information and supporting documentation is received. If the application is incomplete, the applicant will be notified and given an opportunity to provide missing documentation. Once the application is deemed eligible, the applicant will receive a Release for Signature. Once the signed Release is received, the reimbursement check will be processed. The program is administered as part of Baltimore City's compliance efforts under the Modified Sanitary Sewer Consent Decree.

structured_extraction.program_name: FY 2022 CoC Unsheltered Special NOFO Program Competition
structured_extraction.program_description: The Continuum of Care program promotes community-wide commitment to ending homelessness. This special funding opportunity provides grants to nonprofit providers and state and local governments to quickly rehouse homeless individuals and families while minimizing trauma and dislocation. The program promotes access to mainstream programs and optimizes self-sufficiency among individuals and families experiencing homelessness. Through this special notice of funding opportunity, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development awards funding to communities to implement coordinated approaches grounded in Housing First and public health principles to reduce unsheltered homelessness and improve services, health outcomes, and housing stability among highly vulnerable unsheltered individuals and families.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: HUD awards funding to communities to implement coordinated approaches to reduce unsheltered homelessness and improve services and housing stability among vulnerable unsheltered individuals and families. Funding supports new and renewal projects that address the needs of unsheltered populations, with emphasis on Housing First approaches and leveraging mainstream resources.

structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Funding for efforts to quickly rehouse homeless individuals and families, promote access to mainstream programs, and optimize self-sufficiency among individuals and families experiencing homelessness. Supports implementation of Housing First and public health principles.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City
requirements_list: Applicants must partner with health and housing agencies to leverage mainstream housing and healthcare resources
Projects must submit all required materials, including supporting documentation and match documentation
Projects must implement Housing First principles
Projects must coordinate with the Baltimore City CoC
Applications must be submitted by September 16, 2022 at 5:00 pm to HSPApplications@baltimorecity.gov
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Applicants submit new or renewal project applications with all required materials and supporting documentation to HSP Applications by the stated deadline. The Committee selects which projects will be included in the Baltimore City CoC's application to HUD and approves final project ranking. A public notification of ranked projects is posted after the selection process is complete.

structured_extraction.program_description: A competitive grant opportunity that brings together funding from multiple sources to support organizations providing services to individuals and families who are at risk of homelessness, currently homeless, or living with HIV or AIDS in Baltimore City. Organizations submit one application and can be considered for funding from six different funding sources. Both new and renewal project proposals are accepted.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Competitive grants from six funding sources: (1) U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development Emergency Solutions Grant (ESG) - approximately $1,753,633 available for street outreach, emergency shelters, homelessness prevention, rapid re-housing; (2) State of Maryland Homeless Solutions Program (HSP) - approximately $2,968,022 available for street outreach, emergency shelters, homelessness prevention, rapid re-housing; (3) Baltimore City Department of Social Services (DSS) - approximately $314,128 for emergency shelter and supportive services; (4) HUD Housing Opportunities for Persons with AIDS/HIV (HOPWA) - approximately $200,000 available for short-term rent, mortgage, utility assistance, permanent housing placement, employment and education services; (5) Maryland Department of Health State Special Funds (SSF) - approximately $100,000 for housing case management and services for low-income persons living with HIV/AIDS; (6) Baltimore City General Funds - approximately $9,000,000 available for street outreach and emergency shelter. Grant term runs July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2025 (City Fiscal Year 2025). Eligible activities include emergency shelter, transitional housing, housing and services for people with HIV/AIDS, housing stabilization and homelessness prevention, rapid re-housing, street outreach, and permanent supportive housing.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Qualified non-profit organizations and city government agencies serving individuals and families who are at risk of homelessness, currently homeless, or living with HIV or AIDS in Baltimore City.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Funding supports programs in the following categories: emergency shelter, transitional housing, housing and services for people with HIV/AIDS, housing stabilization and homelessness prevention, rapid re-housing, street outreach, permanent supportive housing, eviction prevention, and day centers. Eligible uses depend on funding source and may include short-term rent, mortgage and utility assistance, permanent housing placement, employment and education assistance, childcare services, life skills management, legal services, and housing case management.

structured_extraction.program_name: FY 2025 Continuum of Care (CoC) NOFO Program Competition
structured_extraction.program_description: The Continuum of Care (CoC) program, funded by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), promotes a community-wide commitment to ending homelessness. It provides competitive federal grants to nonprofit providers and state and local governments to quickly rehouse individuals and families experiencing homelessness while minimizing the impacts of trauma and dislocation. The program promotes self-sufficiency and access to mainstream programs, supports a Housing First approach, and funds permanent supportive housing, rapid rehousing, transitional housing, supportive services, and Homeless Management Information System (HMIS) improvements. In Baltimore City, more than 75% of funding supports Permanent Supportive Housing programs that combine long-term housing subsidies with supportive services. HUD announces a Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) each year, after which Baltimore City holds a local competition to select renewal and new projects aligned with HUD's priorities. The program also seeks to address racial inequalities in homelessness and connect individuals with public benefits and employment opportunities.
list_of_relevant_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Competitive federal grants distributed through a local competition process. For FY 2025, Baltimore City CoC has $31,796,073 in Annual Renewal Demand (ARD), $6,359,215 in CoC Bonus Project Funding, $3,142,356 in Domestic Violence Bonus Project Funding, and $1,500,000 in CoC Planning Grant Funds, totaling approximately $42,797,644 available. Funding supports Permanent Supportive Housing (PSH), Rapid Rehousing (RRH), Transitional Housing (TH), Supportive Services Only (SSO), and HMIS projects. Permanent housing projects are capped at 30% of ARD ($9.5 million total). More than 75% of Baltimore City funding is directed to Permanent Supportive Housing programs combining long-term housing subsidies with supportive services. Applications are submitted through the Neighborly portal and are evaluated by the Resource Allocation Committee (RAC) based on HUD priorities, project performance data, and local competition criteria. Local areas typically have 60–75 days to apply once HUD announces the annual NOFO. Projects are selected and ranked by the RAC before submission to HUD.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Nonprofit organizations and state and local government agencies serving homeless populations in Baltimore City, including providers of rapid rehousing, permanent supportive housing, transitional housing, supportive services, and HMIS infrastructure. Organizations that have not previously received CoC funding are also invited to apply.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Quickly rehousing individuals and families experiencing homelessness; minimizing trauma and dislocation; providing permanent supportive housing, rapid rehousing, and transitional housing; supportive services; promoting self-sufficiency, employment, and access to mainstream programs and public benefits; improving the Homeless Management Information System (HMIS); conducting outreach and street engagement; providing coordinated entry services; substance abuse treatment and recovery support; behavioral health services; trauma-informed care; housing assistance (leasing and rental assistance); and supportive services including case management, employment assistance, and specialized services for vulnerable subpopulations including youth, families, domestic violence survivors, and persons with disabilities.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City, Maryland. The program applies to the Baltimore Continuum of Care area (MD-501) and is part of the nationwide HUD Continuum of Care competitive process.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: HUD announces nationwide funding competition each year through a Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO). Once announced, Baltimore City holds a local competition. The process timeline includes: 1) HUD NOFO released (November 13, 2025); 2) Resource Allocation Committee (RAC) Meeting to approve competition guidelines (November 17, 2025); 3) CoC Board votes to approve guidelines (November 18, 2025); 4) Local competition materials released and application period opens (November 19, 2025); 5) Mandatory Bidder's Conference held (November 21, 2025); 6) FAQs posted (November 28, 2025); 7) Application deadline (December 12, 2025, 5:00 pm EST). Applicants create an account on the Neighborly portal, add two organizational points of contact, and have an authorized individual download and complete the appropriate application template (renewal, new and expansion, or YHDP renewal/replacement). The authorized individual uploads all required application materials, supporting documentation, and match commitments, then certifies and submits the application through Neighborly. Neighborly sends an automated confirmation of receipt. HUD Direct Grantees submit applications in e-snaps per HUD procedures. The RAC reviews, scores, and ranks all applications according to local scoring criteria aligned with HUD priorities, which emphasize: 1) Ending the Crisis of Homelessness on Streets; 2) Prioritizing Treatment and Recovery; 3) Advancing Public Safety; 4) Promoting Self-Sufficiency; 5) Improving Outcomes; and 6) Minimizing Trauma. For renewal projects, the RAC reviews performance data and determines which projects may receive reductions or reallocations; for new projects, the RAC assesses quality and alignment with CoC priorities. Applicants are publicly notified of acceptance and ranking at least 15 days prior to HUD submission deadline (December 23, 2025). The final consolidated CoC application is reviewed for public comment (January 8, 2026) and submitted to HUD (January 13, 2026).

structured_extraction.program_description: This program helps first-time homebuyers at or below 80% of the area median income purchase homes in Baltimore City by providing down payment assistance, gap funding to reduce loan balance, and interest rate buydowns.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Eligible first-time homebuyers receive up to 50% of the required down payment, gap funding to reduce the loan balance (calculated as the difference between the annual mortgage payment (PITI) and 30% of annual household income), and an interest rate buydown up to 2.5% of the sales price. An additional $5,000 bonus is available for buyers who (a) purchase a house they have rented and occupied for at least six months, or (b) have a disability or a household member with a disability. Up to 50% of closing costs can be covered using the funds mentioned above. Most assistance is structured as forgivable loans that do not need to be repaid if the homeowner stays in the home for five years. Funds cannot be used to pay realtor fees, and buyers cannot receive cash at the settlement table. Funds are available on a first come, first served basis.
structured_extraction.program_audience: First-time homebuyers in Baltimore City with household income at or below 80% of the area median income
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Down payment assistance, closing cost reduction, loan balance reduction, and interest rate buydowns for home purchases. Funds can be used toward the principal of the mortgage, to buy down the interest rate, or to cover up to 50% of closing costs.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Homes must be located in Baltimore City
requirements_list: Must be a first-time homebuyer

Household income must be at or below 80% of the area median income (FY25 limits: 1 person $72,950; 2 people $83,400; 3 people $93,800; 4 people $104,200; 5 people $112,550; 6 people $120,900; 7 people $129,250; 8 people $137,550)
Must complete homeownership class from a City-approved homeownership counseling agency within one year before purchasing
Must contribute at least $1,000 of own money toward the house
Housing counselor and lender must complete the online application
Settlement date must be at least 30 days after submitting application
Buyers cannot receive the 2.5% interest rate buydown if they are receiving funds from the Maryland Mortgage Program
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Register your account and submit an application through the Applicant Portal at https://portal.neighborlysoftware.com/baltimoremd/Participant. Create a user name (your email address) and password; the system will validate ownership of your email address by sending a validation link. Your housing counselor and lender must also complete the online application. Ensure your settlement date is at least 30 days after submitting your application. Checks are typically sent 10 to 15 business days after approval. You can also use the online calculator at https://cityservices.baltimorecity.gov/fthip to estimate your incentive amount by entering your applicant name, household annual income, loan amount, monthly mortgage payment, and down payment.

structured_extraction.program_name: Historic Rehabilitation and Restoration Tax Credit (CHAP Tax Credit)
structured_extraction.program_description: A 10-year property tax credit program administered by the Commission for Historical and Architectural Preservation (CHAP) that encourages property owners in Baltimore City to complete major rehabilitation and restoration projects on historic structures. The credit is calculated based on the increased property value resulting from qualifying rehabilitation work and appears on the property tax bill as a 'Special Credit.' Both residential and commercial properties are eligible. Since 1997, over $1.3 billion has been invested in historic properties through this program with over 4,300 projects completed.
list_of_relevant_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: A 10-year property tax credit computed based on the increase in property value resulting from qualifying rehabilitation work. The credit equals the difference between the City real property tax on the post-improvement full cash value and the City real property tax on the base year full cash value. For projects with construction costs of $5.0 million or less, the credit is 100% each year for all 10 years. For projects exceeding $5.0 million (for the portion not eligible for Enterprise Zone credit), the credit is phased: Years 1-5 at 80%, Year 6 at 70%, Year 7 at 60%, Year 8 at 50%, Year 9 at 40%, and Year 10 at 30%. The credit is fully transferable to subsequent owners for the remaining life of the credit and continues to apply even if property values increase further. Both residential and commercial properties are eligible. The amount of the credit is calculated by the Department of Finance based on documented rehabilitation costs and post-improvement appraisal value, and appears on the property tax bill as a 'Special Credit.' Property owners must invest at least 25 percent of the property's initial full cash value. Since 1997, over $1.3 billion has been invested in historic properties through this program with over 4,300 projects completed. The credit cannot be used for property acquisition costs, utility bills, property taxes, or holding costs.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Ongoing rolling program; applications must receive final certification within 2 years for projects under $3.5 million or 3 years for projects over $3.5 million, with opportunity for one-time extension of equivalent length.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Property owners in historic districts of Baltimore City, including homeowners and business owners with residential or commercial properties, who want to rehabilitate historically designated buildings. The program applies to both owner-occupied and investor-owned properties.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Qualifying rehabilitation and restoration work on eligible historic properties, including interior and exterior improvements that meet CHAP Design Guidelines. Eligible expenses include architectural design, appraisal, engineering, demolition, site preparation, restoration, alteration, interior and exterior work including all electrical, plumbing, mechanical and related work required to be permitted under Baltimore City Building, Fire and Related codes, and interior and exterior finish work normally associated with historic projects. The credit cannot be used for property acquisition costs, utility bills, property taxes, holding costs, or work that does not meet CHAP Design Guidelines.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City only. The property must be designated as a Baltimore City Landmark, have a National Register Individual Designation, be contributing to a Baltimore City Historic District, contributing to a National Register Historic District, or contributing to the Baltimore National Heritage Area.
requirements_list: Property must be historically designated as a Baltimore City Landmark, National Register Individual Designation, Contributing to a Baltimore City Historic District, Contributing to a National Register Historic District, or Contributing to the Baltimore National Heritage Area
Property must be located in a historic district or be a designated local landmark in Baltimore City
Project must receive preliminary approval from CHAP Staff before any work begins
All work must meet CHAP Design Guidelines
Total investment must be at least 25 percent of the initial full cash value of the property
Applicants must provide thorough color photographs of exterior elevations, roof, interior rooms, and architectural details in high resolution
If any building elevation or interior layout will be altered, applicants must provide existing and proposed drawings
Detailed scope of work must be submitted describing interior and exterior plans, proposed materials, treatments, and alterations
Proof of ownership required such as HUD1, deed, signed purchase agreement, or tax bill
Authorization to Proceed Application required only for properties in local historic districts
Enterprise Zone Verification Form required if property has a commercial component

Pre-improvement appraisal completed by a Certified Residential or General Real Estate Appraiser must be submitted within 90 days of initial application submission and must meet Department of Finance requirements
Post-improvement appraisal completed by a Certified Appraiser must be submitted within 90 days of issuance of final Use and Occupancy Permit or last permit inspection
Cost documentation must be notarized and list all rehabilitation-related expenses totaling at least 25 percent of full cash value, with only actual paid costs accepted, not estimates
Copies of all permits including Use and Occupancy Permit if required must be submitted upon completion
Photographs of completed rehabilitation corresponding to original application photos must be submitted in final certification
Projects must be completed within two years for projects under $3.5 million dollars or three years for projects over $3.5 million dollars, with opportunity for one-time extension of equivalent length

No work shall be undertaken prior to obtaining preliminary approval from CHAP; any work begun before application submittal or before CHAP preliminary approval is issued renders the property ineligible
No work may be undertaken between application submission and issuance of preliminary approval without express written permission from CHAP
Initial appraisal must be completed before any work begins on the property

For projects over $3.5 million, applicants must provide documentation reviewed with the State Department of Assessments and Taxation regarding preliminary estimate of value, a statement of projected economic impact and public benefits including neighborhood revitalization, job creation, tax generation, and minority business development, and certification from Baltimore Development Corporation regarding Enterprise Zone eligibility

For projects over $3.5 million, applicants must provide proof that existing building was at least 75% vacant for at least three years, OR documentation supporting high-performance market-rate rental housing project status, OR other evidence demonstrating necessity of credit for project to proceed
For projects over $3.5 million, applicants must provide actual economic impact statement within 3-4 years of application acceptance
Property owner must maintain major historic features and comply with City Building, Fire and Related Codes throughout the 10-year credit term to maintain continuing eligibility

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: 1. Determine if your property is eligible by checking the Historic Tax Credit Eligible mapping layer on the city website or verifying the property meets historic designation criteria (Baltimore City Landmark, National Register Individual Designation, Contributing to a Baltimore City Historic District, Contributing to a National Register Historic District, or Contributing to the Baltimore National Heritage Area). 2. Read the Tax Credit FAQ and review the Program Rules and Regulations and CHAP Design Guidelines. 3. Prepare required application materials including: thorough high-resolution color photographs of exterior elevations, roof, interior rooms, and architectural details; existing and proposed drawings if any building elevation or interior layout will be altered; detailed scope of work describing interior and exterior plans, proposed materials, treatments, and alterations; proof of ownership (HUD1, deed, signed purchase agreement, or tax bill); pre-improvement appraisal by a Certified Appraiser conforming to program requirements; any required forms (Authorization to Proceed for local historic district properties, Enterprise Zone Verification Form if applicable). 4. Submit the online application through the Historic Tax Credit Application system at propertytaxcredits.baltimorecity.gov with the application fee (amount set by Board of Estimates) paid online. All applications and documents must be submitted electronically via the System; no paper applications are accepted. 5. CHAP reviews the application for preliminary approval to ensure proposed work meets Baltimore City Historic Preservation Design Guidelines. Applications must receive preliminary approval within 180 days of submission or are deemed expired. Preliminary certification is issued in writing and submitted to the Director of Finance. 6. Once preliminary approval is received from CHAP, begin rehabilitation project according to CHAP Design Guidelines and approved plans. Projects with construction costs under $3.5 million must be completed within 2 years of preliminary approval; projects over $3.5 million must be completed within 3 years. One-time extension of equivalent length available upon request before expiration. 7. Upon project completion, obtain all required permits and Use and Occupancy Permit (if required). 8. Submit final certification materials through the online system including: final photographs corresponding to original application photos; copies of all permits and inspection certificates; notarized cost documentation listing all rehabilitation-related expenses totaling at least 25% of full cash value with only actual paid costs (not estimates); post-improvement appraisal by a Certified Appraiser submitted within 90 days of final Use and Occupancy Permit or last permit inspection. 9. Final certification request must be submitted within 180 days or is deemed expired. CHAP reviews completed work to ensure it conforms to approved plans and meets Design Guidelines. 10. CHAP provides final certification to Director of Finance via the System. 11. Tax credit is calculated by Department of Finance based on difference between pre-improvement and post-improvement full cash values and current City tax rates. 12. Tax credit appears on the next issued property tax bill as a 'Special Credit' and continues for 10 years. 13. For projects over $3.5 million, provide actual economic impact statement within 3-4 years of application acceptance. Contact historictaxcredit@baltimorecity.gov for questions.

structured_extraction.program_name: Housing Opportunities for Persons with HIV/AIDS (HOPWA) Program
structured_extraction.program_description: HOPWA is a federal program administered by Baltimore City that supports persons living with HIV/AIDS and their families by providing safe, sanitary, and stable housing and a range of supportive services. The program funds both direct housing assistance to eligible individuals and competitive grants to project sponsors (non-profit organizations and city agencies) serving people living with HIV/AIDS. HOPWA aims to help participants find quality housing, maintain housing stability, gain better access to care, and enhance quality of life. Funding is distributed annually based on community needs and priorities across the Baltimore-Towson Eligible Metropolitan Statistical Area (EMSA).
structured_extraction.assistance_description: HOPWA provides two primary forms of assistance: (1) Direct housing assistance to eligible individuals including tenant-based or project-based rental assistance, conversion and repair of facilities, new construction, and short-term payments for rent, mortgage, and utilities to prevent homelessness; and (2) Competitive grants awarded annually to project sponsors (non-profit organizations and city agencies) that provide housing and support services to people living with HIV/AIDS. Supportive services include permanent housing placement, employment and education services, personal assistance, help accessing benefits, and resources for drug and alcohol treatment, daycare, nutritional services, intensive care, and physical and mental health services. The City of Baltimore annually contracts with localities within the Baltimore-Towson EMSA to provide tenant-based rental assistance and support services. Award amounts vary based on project type and community need.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Department of Housing and Community Development in Baltimore City helps eligible owner-occupants repair and rehabilitate their homes. The program assists with emergency and safety repairs for homeowners who lack sufficient financial resources. Assistance covers repairs such as roof repairs, heating system repairs, plumbing repairs, electrical work, lead hazard remediation, and accessibility improvements for people with disabilities. Help is available in the form of loans (which may be forgiven or have delayed repayment depending on circumstances) and grants for lead remediation and accessibility improvements.

structured_extraction.assistance_description: Assistance is provided through loans that must be repaid, with some loans subject to forgiveness or deferral depending on circumstances. Forgivable loans are forgiven after five years if the applicant lives in the home as their primary residence during that time. Deferred loans are due back to the City when the property is sold and are paid from the profit of the sale. Grants are also available for specific purposes such as lead remediation and accessibility improvements for people with disabilities. Grants do not require repayment but applicants must meet eligibility requirements. Funding helps low-income homeowners repair or replace roofs, heating systems, plumbing, electrical systems, and address other emergency and safety problems in their homes.

structured_extraction.program_description: A local policy requiring developers of qualifying residential rental projects to include affordable housing units as part of their projects when the project receives a benefit from the city such as a tax credit, grant, or significant land use authorization. Projects must make 10% of their units available as affordable rental units for a 30-year period, with 5% available to households earning 50% of area median income and 5% available to households earning 60% of area median income. Tenants pay the maximum affordable rent established by HUD, with the difference between market rate and affordable rent covered by the High-Performance Inclusionary Housing Tax Credit administered by the City's Finance Department. The policy applies to new buildings, major renovations, and conversions from non-residential use costing more than $60,000 per unit with 20 or more housing units, for building permits submitted on or after July 21, 2024.
list_of_eligible_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
list_of_relevant_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Developers of qualifying rental housing projects must make 10% of units affordable for a 30-year period commencing when the City issues a Certificate of Use and Occupancy. Five percent of inclusionary units must be available to households earning 50% of area median income (low-income) and 5% must be available to households earning 60% of area median income (very low-income). The difference between market rate rent and affordable rent is covered by the High-Performance Inclusionary Housing Tax Credit (City Code Article 28, Section 10-18.2) or economically equivalent consideration administered by the City's Finance Department. Affordable rent is set at HUD-established maximum affordable rent levels. The requirement applies to projects with 20 or more units (excluding penthouse units) that receive a major public subsidy or benefit from significant land use authorization and involve new construction, wholly renovated buildings, or conversion from non-residential use costing more than $60,000 per unit. Developers may offer additional subsidy to provide up to an additional 5% of units (maximum 15% total) to extremely low-income and very low-income households.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Ongoing - applications accepted at time of building permit submission
structured_extraction.program_audience: Developers and builders of market rate rental housing projects that receive a major public subsidy or benefit from significant land use authorization, undertaking residential housing projects of 20 or more units in Baltimore City.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Creation and construction of affordable rental housing units within market rate residential projects, with rents set at affordable levels for households earning 50% to 60% of area median income for a 30-year period. Inclusionary units must be designed and planned at the same time as market rate units, have the same exterior appearance, number of bedrooms, and overall quality of construction as comparable market rate units, and offer the same amenities as market rate tenants.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City only
requirements_list: Project must include 20 or more housing units (penthouse units are excluded from this calculation)
Project must receive a major public subsidy OR benefit from significant land use authorization
Project must be newly constructed, wholly renovated, or converted from non-residential housing use
Cost of construction or conversion must exceed $60,000 per unit
Building permit application must be submitted on or after July 21, 2024
Project must submit an Inclusionary Housing Plan at time of building permit application following Section 2B-22(A) of City Ordinance 24-308

Inclusionary Housing Plan must include general project information, confirmation that the project meets all four criteria, project description, site plan showing unit locations, unit identification table with rental rates, project schedule, and Affirmative Marketing Plan
10% of units must be made affordable: 5% to households at 50% AMI (low-income) and 5% to households at 60% AMI (very low-income)
Affordable units must remain affordable for a 30-year period beginning when the City issues a Certificate of Use and Occupancy
Inclusionary units must have floorplans provided in the same proportion as market rate units throughout the building
Inclusionary units may not be grouped in concentration on a particular floor or within a particular building if project includes multiple buildings
Inclusionary units must be designed with same exterior appearance, number of bedrooms, and overall quality of construction as comparable market rate units
Inclusionary units must include same amenities as market rate units, with fee-based amenities offered at same price as market rate tenants
Size variation for inclusionary units permitted up to maximum of 10% from comparable market rate unit
Developer must ensure tenant of inclusionary unit meets income requirements verified using most recent annual household income and HUD maximum AMI limits
Developer must reverify tenant household income annually when lease is renewed

Affirmative Marketing Plan must be written in plain English, include non-discrimination practices, reasonable accommodation process for disabilities, application availability procedures, waitlist maintenance, prohibition on income and credit score requirements for applicants with rental assistance, procedures for credit score mitigation, criminal record screening policy, and application denial notification process with specific reasons
Eviction records older than 3 years may not be included in tenant screening or affirmative marketing plan
Developers may not include evictions in screening where tenant prevailed, settlement was reached, or matter was dropped
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Developers submit an Inclusionary Housing Plan when applying for a building permit on or after July 21, 2024. The plan must be submitted electronically with time and date stamp to the address specified on the form and must include general project information, confirmation that the project meets all four eligibility criteria, project description, site plan, unit identification table with market and affordable rental rates, project schedule, and an Affirmative Marketing Plan. The Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) conducts an initial review within 10 business days and may request additional information or changes. The developer has 5 business days to submit requested materials. DHCD then proceeds to approval or denial. Upon review of a complete plan, DHCD provides a recommendation to the Inclusionary Housing Board. The Board meets within 15 business days of receipt to provide comments. DHCD provides written response to developer within 45 business days of submission stating whether the plan is approved or denied and whether a building permit may be issued. No building permit is released without an approved Inclusionary Housing Plan. Following approval, the inclusionary housing program manager sends written notification to the Department's Permits and Plans Review Office. Approved plans are posted on DHCD's website. Developers may submit technical modifications (changes to project name, contact information, or address) via email. Non-technical modifications follow the full review process and may not result in fewer required inclusionary units.

structured_extraction.program_description: The City of Baltimore provides seed money for one-time investments that improve results, increase revenue, or reduce ongoing operating costs for City services. Savings from successful investments are returned to the fund to support future projects.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Agencies may apply for seed funding to invest in innovative projects. Proposals submitted during the annual budget process may be included in the agency's annual budget. Proposals received later in the fiscal year are assessed on a rolling basis. Proposals are evaluated on a 100-point scale based on: clarity of project intentions and benefits, business case and repayment plan, risk identification and mitigation, success metrics and performance measures, equity impact, financial planning with itemized costs, partnership leveraging, and writing quality. Successful projects are expected to repay the investment through cost savings, new revenue, or a combination of both.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Rolling basis during the fiscal year or during the annual budget process
structured_extraction.program_audience: City of Baltimore agency heads and staff with project ideas that lead to improved results, increased revenue, or reduced operating costs. City agencies or quasi-City agencies are eligible; grantees are not eligible but can partner with eligible agencies.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Seed money for one-time investments in projects that improve city services, increase revenue, or reduce ongoing operating costs. Projects must demonstrate a business case for repayment through cost savings, new revenue, or both.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City
requirements_list: City agency or quasi-City agency status (grantees ineligible but may partner with eligible agencies)
Submit detailed proposal including all required sections completely filled
Include project description with key benefits for agency, customers, and the City
Include implementation plan with resources needed (human, social, organizational, physical, technological), project timeline, and risk analysis
Include evaluation plan defining overall goals, success metrics, performance measures, and discussion of equity impact
Include detailed budget with one-time and future costs itemized and described
Indicate whether investment will be repaid via cost savings, new revenue, or both
Include proposal signatures from project manager(s), fiscal officer, and agency head
Proposals must be kept to less than 150 words for free response questions
Incomplete applications will not be considered
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Step 1: Prepare a complete proposal using the Innovation Fund Investment Proposal template, including all seven sections: General Information, Primary Contacts/Project Managers, Project Description, Implementation Plan, Evaluation, Budget, and Acknowledgment and Approval. Step 2: Proposals can be submitted during the annual budget process (eligible for inclusion in annual budget) or on a rolling basis during the fiscal year. Step 3: Submit completed proposal with original signatures to Aaron.Moore@baltimorecity.gov. Step 4: Proposals are evaluated by a Review Team including staff from Bureau of the Budget and Management Research (BBMR), CitiStatSMART, Baltimore City IT (BCIT), and the Mayor's Office using a standardized 100-point rating sheet assessing project clarity, business case, risk management, performance measures, equity impact, financial planning, partnerships, and writing quality. Step 5: Successful proposals are awarded funding with expectation of repayment through cost savings or revenue generation.

structured_extraction.program_description: Judicial In Rem Foreclosure is a process that enables the Baltimore City Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) to foreclose on liens (unpaid property taxes, environmental citations, water bills, etc.) for vacant lots or buildings where the total liens exceed the property's assessed value. This approach allows the city to systematically acquire abandoned properties, block by block, and work with communities to determine their future use — including redevelopment by homeowners, small developers, community development organizations, and other interested parties — thereby addressing properties that negatively impact neighborhood conditions.
list_of_relevant_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The City acquires vacant lots and vacant buildings through judicial foreclosure of liens (including unpaid property taxes, environmental citations, water bills, and similar obligations) where those liens exceed the assessed property value. Once the City takes title through court award, properties can be offered for redevelopment without requiring an auction, and can be made available to homeowners, small developers, community development organizations, developers, or other interested parties. DHCD will work with communities to determine the best outcomes for properties or groupings of properties. The average time to complete an in rem case from filing to judgment is approximately 6-8 months (177 days). As of October 2023, there were approximately 13,795 vacant and abandoned properties with Vacant Building Notices in Baltimore City, of which the City owned 963.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Rolling/Ongoing - Communities can submit properties at any time
structured_extraction.program_audience: Communities, homeowners, small developers, community development organizations, and other developers interested in acquiring and redeveloping vacant properties in Baltimore City, as well as the Baltimore City government itself as a tool for systematically addressing abandoned properties.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Acquisition of vacant lots and buildings through judicial foreclosure of liens, enabling the city to gain ownership and make properties available for redevelopment to meet community needs and goals as determined by community participation and planning.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Vacant lots or buildings in Baltimore City with Vacant Building Notices where municipal liens exceed the assessed property value. Baltimore City only.
requirements_list: Property must be a vacant lot or have a Vacant Building Notice (VBN)
Property must be vacant or abandoned
Municipal liens must exceed the assessed value of the property
Liens may include unpaid property taxes, environmental citations, water bills, and similar obligations
No active tax sale certificate holder for the property
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Communities can submit property addresses to DHCD using the In Rem Eligibility Form (https://dhcd.baltimorecity.gov/rem-eligibility-form) for review. DHCD will complete analysis to determine if the property qualifies for Judicial In Rem foreclosure. If the property qualifies, DHCD files a case in Circuit Court and provides proper notice to any person with a legal interest in the property. If liens are not paid and foreclosure is not successfully contested, the court awards title to the City. The process typically takes 6-8 months from filing to title award. Communities can also call 311 to request a Vacant Building Inspection for properties without high liens; if a Vacant Building Notice (VBN) is issued and not abated, a citation of $900 is issued (proposed to increase to $1,000 per violation, with each day of non-compliance being a new violation).

structured_extraction.program_description: A coordination service that helps Baltimore City residents access free or low-cost services to make their homes safer, healthier, and more comfortable. LIGHT Coordinators assess residents' needs and connect them with programs like home repairs, energy savings, and lead hazard removal.
list_of_relevant_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free coordination and assessment services to connect residents with available home repair, energy efficiency, lead hazard reduction, and weatherization programs. LIGHT Coordinators work with residents to identify needs and link them to appropriate assistance. Three grant and loan programs are available: (1) Home Rehabilitation Program for emergency repairs, code violations, and health/safety issues; (2) Lead Hazard Reduction Program for lead-based paint remediation and treatment (for eligible residents with pregnant women or children under age 6); (3) Weatherization Program for energy efficiency improvements. Some programs provide grants, while others offer forgivable loans (forgiven after 5 years if primary residence maintained) or deferred loans (due when property is sold). Income limits apply based on household size, ranging from $66,300 (1-person household) to $124,950 (8-person household), with $13,450 for each additional household member.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Low-income homeowners and renters in Baltimore City who need help making their homes safer, healthier, and more comfortable. Single-point access for residents seeking home repair, energy efficiency, lead hazard reduction, and weatherization assistance.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Home repairs including emergency fixes, roof repairs, heating systems, plumbing, electrical systems, sewer and water line repairs; energy efficiency improvements including insulation, air sealing, weatherstripping, HVAC maintenance, heating system maintenance/replacement, pipe wraps, and light bulbs; lead hazard reduction including paint treatment, door/window treatment, floor treatment, paint elimination, stabilization and repainting, and other lead risk reduction measures; accessibility modifications for people with disabilities.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available to residents of Baltimore City only.
requirements_list: Must be a resident of Baltimore City
Household income within program limits: $66,300-$124,950 based on household size (1-8 persons), plus $13,450 per additional household member
For lead hazard reduction: pregnant woman or child under age 6 must be part of household or spend more than 10 hours per week in home

For homeowners: deed must be in applicant's name; current on mortgage payments (if applicable); no outstanding judgments; no bankruptcy in last 7 years; no foreclosure efforts; have homeowner's insurance; current on ground rent and property taxes (if applicable); property must be primary residence
For renters: landlord must cooperate with program
Home must have basic utilities functioning (electricity, running water, heating system operational)
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact LIGHT Intake & Assessment Unit at (410) 396-3023 or visit https://dhcd.baltimorecity.gov/hho/light to schedule an assessment. Complete the pre-application form (available online at https://portal.neighborlysoftware.com/BALTIMOREMD/participant or by mail). LIGHT Coordinators will evaluate needs and determine eligibility for available programs. Once pre-application is submitted, applicants may be requested to submit full application and supporting documents for specific programs. After review, program administrators will determine final eligibility. Some programs have waiting lists. A case manager will help coordinate services for which applicant is eligible. Applications can be submitted through the online portal or by mail using the pre-application form.

structured_extraction.program_name: Legacy Homeowners Pilot Program (Tax Debt Elimination)
structured_extraction.program_description: A $2 million pilot program that eliminates property tax debt for eligible legacy residents of Baltimore City who are 65 or older, have owned their home for at least 10 years, make $73,000 or less annually, and are at risk for tax sale. Qualifying homeowners will have their property tax debt forgiven through the Tax Sale Coordination and Prevention Services program. Applicants must have received a Final Bill and Legal Notices (FBLN) in February, have a home assessed value of $250,000 or less, own their home as a primary residence, and agree to enter into a payment plan for future tax year bills. Funding is limited to $2 million total (awarded on a first-come, first-served basis per applicant's tax lien amount), and once exhausted, the program will close.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Property tax debt is forgiven for qualifying legacy homeowners through the Tax Sale Coordination and Prevention Services program. The program allocates a one-time total of $2 million in Fiscal Year 2027 budget. Each applicant's tax lien amount is subtracted from this total on a first-come, first-served basis. Once the $2 million is exhausted, the program closes. Participants must agree to enter into a payment plan for future tax year bills. Eligibility requires: being 65 or older, having owned the home for at least 10 years as a primary residence, making $73,000 or less in combined household income for the 2025 tax year, having a home assessed value of $250,000 or less, being at risk for tax sale, and having received a Final Bill and Legal Notices (FBLN) in February. Applicants must enroll in the Baltimore City Tax Sale Deferral Program by April 15, 2026.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: By April 15, 2026, while funding allows, first-come first serve
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore City residents who are 65 or older, have owned their home for at least 10 years as a primary residence, make $73,000 or less in combined household income for the 2025 tax year, have a home assessed value of $250,000 or less, are at risk for tax sale (received Final Bill and Legal Notices in February), and will enroll in or are already enrolled in the Baltimore City Tax Sale Deferral Program.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Forgiveness of property tax debt for legacy homeowners; elimination of tax liens.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Applicants can enroll in the Tax Sale Deferral Program, which opened February 15, 2026. Apply online at https://bit.ly/DHCD-Neighborly or submit a hard copy application available at https://bit.ly/TaxDeferralHardCopy. Hard copy applications can also be picked up at the 1st floor of the Abel Wolman Building or the 11th floor of 417 E. Fayette Street, Baltimore, 21202. For homeowners aged 65 and older who do not qualify for Tax Sale Deferral but meet Legacy Homeowners Pilot requirements (owned home longer than 10 years, combined household income less than $73,000), complete the Tax Sale Deferral form online and indicate you are applying for the Legacy Homeowners Pilot. In-person sign-up assistance is available at the Waxter Senior Center on April 10th, 2026. Bring government-issued ID, 2 utility bills addressed to the property, and proof of income for tax year 2025. The Mayor's Office of Older Adult Affairs and Advocacy conducts coordinated in-person and phone outreach through the deadline.

structured_extraction.program_description: This partnership program with participating employers encourages homeownership near places of employment by matching employer contributions to provide incentives for workers who buy homes in Baltimore City.

structured_extraction.program_description: A job and career support program for people recovering from substance use disorder in Baltimore. The program also provides education to local businesses about substance use disorder and helps them build supportive work environments.

The exemption is valid for one year and must be renewed annually by reapplying with updated medical certification.

structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Protects water and sewer service from being shut off for medical necessity

Provide proof of address such as utility bill, credit card bill, bank statement, or lease/mortgage document

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Download or request the Medical Exemption application form.
